title: Man Owns 400 Jeeps and Still Says, “No, I Don’t Have A Problem”

body_markdown:
A lifetime of playing with old cars can lead to the accumulation of a lot of things: stories, automobilia, spare parts, tools, scars, and, sometimes, a hell of a lot of cars. Or, more specifically,[Jeeps](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/when-overbuilt-is-just-right-for-a-vintage-jeep/) , in the case of Mick Mitchell. And by “a hell of a lot” we mean he stopped counting in the mid 200s. Now the collection appears to be nearly double that number.


Mitchell is, like many of us, a person who found something interesting several years ago and then never stopped thinking about it. Early military GPWs and MBs caught his eye when he was a young boy watching newsreels from the battlefields of the Second World War, and seeing the durable, purpose-built machines carrying troops and materiel left an impression. By the eighth grade, Mitchell had a Jeep of his own. Then, it just, well, never stopped, as shown in this video from[Nebraska Public Media](https://youtu.be/pfVibF2h-Wk?si=MS41Vk0LRjX1LxPU) on YouTube.


A career as an architect enabled Mitchell to amass a collection of Jeeps and design the building that would come to house all of them. He counts it as a point of pride that while there are a lot of Jeeps, and many appear just to be sitting and waiting, they are sitting and waiting while sheltered from the elements, something that goes a long way to ensuring that, if and when these Jeeps get called back into service— even for parade duty—they will be in a condition worth saving.


The whole collection is not a military museum or tribute to the effect the Jeep had on the war effort. Instead, Mitchell says it is about the evolution of the Jeep and how it grew to fill so many other uses. Hidden in the rows and rows of flat fenders are early military production models from before the now-iconic stamped grille became common, along with cutaways to show how the engine works. Even at a passing glance, it appears he might have one of every Jeep.


Is a collection like this over the top? Of course it is, but at the same time, who better to assemble an over-the-top collection of one brand than someone who has been a fan of that brand for nearly 80 years? People like Mitchell are crazy, but we are inclined to call it the best kind of crazy.


A mix of old and new (or at least newer) Jeeps fill the large building.
